title: Cryptocurrency
content: A cryptocurrency is a digital or virtual currency secured by cryptography, typically running on a decentralized network such as a blockchain. Unlike fiat currency issued by central banks, most cryptocurrencies have no central issuer; supply rules are enforced by protocol code and network consensus. Ownership is proven by possession of private keys rather than by an account at a financial institution.

title: Blockchain
content: A blockchain is a distributed, append-only ledger in which data is organized into blocks that are cryptographically chained to one another. Each block references the hash of the previous block, making historical records tamper-evident: altering an old block would invalidate every subsequent block. Nodes in the network validate and agree on new blocks through a consensus mechanism such as proof of work or proof of stake.

title: Smart Contract
content: A smart contract is a program stored and executed on a blockchain. It runs deterministically: given the same inputs, every node computes the same result, so no intermediary is needed to enforce the terms. Smart contracts control digital assets directly and are the building blocks of decentralized applications, but they are only as secure as their code — a bug in a smart contract can be exploited automatically, with no human to stop it.

title: Decentralized Application (dApp)
content: A decentralized application, or dApp, is an application whose backend logic runs on a blockchain through smart contracts instead of on a centralized server. Users typically interact through a web or mobile frontend while funds and state live on-chain. dApps inherit blockchain properties such as censorship resistance and transparency, but also inherit its costs: every state change requires a transaction and network fees.

title: Private Key / Public Key
content: A private key is a secret number that authorizes transactions from a wallet; whoever holds it controls the funds. The corresponding public key (and derived address) is safe to share and is what others use to send you assets. Losing the private key permanently locks the funds; sharing it with anyone gives them full control. This is why seed phrases and private keys must never be stored online or given to anyone claiming to be support.

title: Seed Phrase (Recovery Phrase)
content: A seed phrase, also called a recovery phrase or mnemonic, is a sequence of 12 to 24 words from a standard wordlist (BIP-39) that encodes a wallet's private keys. The phrase can regenerate every address and key in the wallet, so it is the ultimate backup and the ultimate attack target. Anyone who obtains the seed phrase can steal all funds across all chains controlled by that wallet, regardless of any password or PIN applied to the wallet app.

title: EOA vs Contract Account
content: On Ethereum and other EVM chains there are two account types. An externally owned account (EOA) is controlled by a private key held by a person or application and can initiate transactions. A contract account is controlled by its code: it can only act when a transaction or internal call triggers it, and it holds balances and logic. Distinguishing the two matters for security — an EOA 'owner' of a token contract is a single point of failure, while a contract-based owner (multisig, timelock) adds checks.

title: Gas
content: Gas is the unit that measures computational work in EVM transactions. Every operation — from simple transfers to complex contract calls — costs a fixed amount of gas, and the sender pays gas price (usually in gwei) multiplied by gas used. A transaction with too low a gas limit fails and reverts, but the fees for the attempted execution are still paid. Gas mechanics are a common source of confusion and a target for scams that promise to 'refund' gas.

title: Mempool
content: The mempool is the pool of pending, not-yet-confirmed transactions on a blockchain network. When a user broadcasts a transaction, it sits in the mempool until a validator or miner includes it in a block. Because mempool contents are visible to network participants, bots can watch for large swaps and front-run them (see MEV and sandwich attacks). Private mempools and direct-to-validator submission exist to hide transactions from public mempool surveillance.

title: Transaction Confirmation / Finality
content: A confirmation is a block containing a transaction, plus every block built on top of it. Each additional confirmation makes a reorg (reversal) harder. Different chains have different finality models: proof-of-work chains such as Bitcoin treat a transaction as practically final after several confirmations, while proof-of-stake chains with finalized checkpoints (e.g. Ethereum after the Merge) provide near-instant finality. Scammers exploit user impatience by asking for payment confirmation of a single, unconfirmed or 0-confirmation transaction.

title: Decentralized Exchange (DEX)
content: A decentralized exchange (DEX) lets users trade tokens directly from their wallets through smart contracts, without a central custodian or order book. Most DEXs use automated market maker (AMM) pools where price is set by the ratio of reserves. Advantages include self-custody and open access; risks include impermanent loss, slippage on thin pools, and smart-contract exploits. Rug-pull tokens are typically only tradable on DEXs, because centralized exchanges perform listing due diligence.

title: Centralized Exchange (CEX)
content: A centralized exchange (CEX) is a trading platform that holds customer funds in its own wallets and matches orders on an internal order book. Examples include major global platforms; the model offers convenience, fiat on-ramps and high liquidity. The trade-off is counterparty risk: users do not control the keys, so an exchange hack, freeze or insolvency (as with FTX) can mean loss of funds. 'Not your keys, not your coins' captures the core risk.

title: Coin vs Token
content: A coin is the native asset of its own blockchain, used for paying transaction fees and securing the network (e.g. BTC, ETH, SOL). A token is a smart-contract asset built on top of an existing chain (e.g. USDC on Ethereum, meme coins on Solana). Coins are required for network operation; tokens represent assets, utility, governance rights or claims. The distinction matters for safety analysis because token contracts can contain custom transfer logic such as taxes, blacklists or hidden mint functions.

title: Stablecoin
content: A stablecoin is a token designed to hold a stable value, usually pegged to a fiat currency such as the U.S. dollar. The main designs are fiat-backed (reserves held by a custodian), crypto-backed (over-collateralized on-chain positions) and algorithmic (supply adjusted by code with little or no backing). Fiat-backed coins are the most common but rely on the issuer's honesty; algorithmic stablecoins have repeatedly failed, most notoriously Terra's UST in May 2022.

title: Wrapped Token
content: A wrapped token represents another asset on a different chain, typically 1:1, so the original asset can be used in that chain's DeFi ecosystem. For example, wETH is ERC-20 wrapped ETH, and bridged assets like wBTC or solBTC represent Bitcoin on other chains. Wrapping requires a custodian or bridge to hold the underlying asset; if that custodian is compromised, the wrapped token can become unbacked. Always verify the wrapper's backing and audit history.

title: Token Standard (ERC-20 / SPL)
content: A token standard is a technical specification that makes tokens interoperable within an ecosystem. ERC-20 is the dominant Ethereum standard (name, symbol, decimals, transfer and allowance functions); SPL is the Solana equivalent; BEP-20, ARC-20 and others exist on other chains. Standards guarantee wallet and DEX compatibility, but they do not guarantee safety: a token can comply with a standard and still contain malicious transfer restrictions or hidden minting.

title: Whitepaper
content: A whitepaper is a project's technical document describing its problem, solution, token economics and roadmap. Historically, quality whitepapers signaled serious projects, but today a whitepaper is easy to fake and many scams publish polished documents that copy legitimate projects. When evaluating a project, treat the whitepaper as marketing material and verify its claims against the actual code, team history and on-chain data.

title: Airdrop
content: An airdrop distributes free tokens, usually to reward early users, promote a project or bootstrap liquidity. Legitimate airdrops are announced by the project and require no payment or seed-phrase sharing. Airdrop scams are extremely common: fake sites claim you must 'connect your wallet to claim' or 'pay gas first' — both are wallet-drainer techniques. The safe rule is that no legitimate airdrop ever asks for your private key or for an advance payment.

title: Automated Market Maker (AMM)
content: An automated market maker (AMM) is a DEX design that prices assets algorithmically from liquidity pools instead of an order book. The classic constant-product formula x*y=k keeps the product of two reserve balances constant, so price moves with the ratio of reserves. Concentrated-liquidity AMMs (Uniswap v3 style) let liquidity providers concentrate capital in price ranges for better efficiency. AMMs are vulnerable to price manipulation when pools are shallow and to impermanent loss for providers.

title: Liquidity Pool (LP)
content: A liquidity pool is a smart-contract-held reserve of tokens that powers an AMM. Users deposit token pairs and receive LP tokens representing their share of the pool; fees from trades are distributed proportionally. Risks to providers include impermanent loss (price divergence between the deposited pair) and pool exploits. For token-safety analysis, the crucial checks are whether LP tokens are burned or locked, how long any lock lasts, and how concentrated the pool is.

title: Impermanent Loss
content: Impermanent loss is the temporary loss of value a liquidity provider suffers when the prices of the deposited assets diverge from the ratio at deposit time. The larger the divergence, the larger the loss relative to simply holding the assets; the loss becomes 'permanent' only if the provider withdraws while prices are still diverged. High-fee pools and stablecoin pairs mitigate it. It is a core reason why high-APY LP farms are not free money.

title: DeFi Lending and Borrowing
content: DeFi lending protocols (Aave, Compound and similar) let users supply assets to earn interest or borrow assets against collateral. Loans are over-collateralized: borrowers must post collateral worth more than the loan, and a health factor below 1 triggers liquidation, where the collateral is sold at a penalty. Because liquidation is automated, sharp price drops can cascade. Users should never treat a borrowing position as risk-free, and should watch utilization and liquidation thresholds.

title: Yield Farming / Liquidity Mining
content: Yield farming (liquidity mining) is the practice of earning rewards, usually in a protocol's native token, by supplying liquidity or staking assets. High advertised APYs are typically paid in newly minted tokens whose price can collapse, making real yield much lower than nominal. Common risks are impermanent loss, smart-contract exploits, and 'reward-token dumping'. Unsustainably high APY (thousands of percent) with anonymous teams and no audits is a classic rug-pull setup.

title: Staking and Liquid Staking
content: Staking locks tokens in a proof-of-stake network or protocol to secure it and earn rewards. Native staking usually locks the asset for a period; liquid staking (e.g. stETH) issues a derivative token that represents the staked position and can be used in DeFi, freeing the capital. Risks include validator slashing, protocol bugs, and de-pegging of the liquid-staking derivative. Verify the validator set and the protocol's slashing history before staking.

title: Cross-Chain Bridge
content: A bridge transfers assets between blockchains, usually by locking tokens on the source chain and minting wrapped tokens on the destination chain, or by moving liquidity through pooled reserves. Bridges are among the most exploited systems in crypto (Ronin ~$620M, Wormhole ~$326M, Nomad ~$190M). Key risk factors are small/centralized validator sets, unverified message-verification logic, upgradeable contracts without timelocks, and a prior exploit history. Prefer well-audited, battle-tested bridges for large amounts.

title: Price Oracle
content: A price oracle supplies off-chain or on-chain price data to smart contracts. Centralized single-source oracles are manipulation targets: an attacker can move the reported price by trading on a thin pool or exploiting a stale feed, then drain a protocol that trusts it. Safer designs use decentralized aggregators (Chainlink-style), TWAP (time-weighted average price) from DEXs, or multi-source validation. Oracle manipulation is a leading cause of DeFi exploits and of fake-token price pumping.

title: Market Capitalization (Market Cap)
content: Market cap for a crypto asset is price multiplied by circulating supply. It is a rough size metric, not a measure of value: two tokens can have the same market cap while one has nearly all supply held by insiders. Always compare market cap against fully diluted valuation (FDV), liquidity and volume. Scam tokens often show tiny market caps relative to their claimed ecosystem, or inflated caps via wash trading on thin pools.

title: Fully Diluted Valuation (FDV)
content: Fully diluted valuation multiplies price by the maximum possible token supply, including tokens that are locked, vesting, or not yet minted. FDV reveals how much a token could be worth if all supply were circulating, exposing the dilution overhang. A large gap between market cap and FDV means future unlock pressure that can depress price. Unlocks are a common sell-the-news event that naive buyers discover too late.

title: Liquidity
content: Liquidity measures how easily an asset can be bought or sold without moving its price. On DEXs, liquidity is the depth of the pool; on CEXs, it is order-book depth. Low liquidity means high slippage and makes price manipulation cheap — a whale or bot can move the price with a small order. Rug-pull tokens typically have shallow, easily drained liquidity. A healthy token has liquidity comparable to or exceeding its daily trading volume.

title: Slippage
content: Slippage is the difference between the expected price of a trade and the price actually executed, caused by trade size relative to available liquidity. High slippage signals a thin market. Scam and honeypot tokens often have extreme buy/sell slippage because the contract manipulates effective prices or because the pool is tiny. Always check the slippage a transaction would incur and set a sane slippage limit before swapping.

title: Market Order vs Limit Order
content: A market order executes immediately at the best available price; a limit order executes only at a specified price or better. Market orders guarantee execution but not price; limit orders guarantee price but not execution. In volatile crypto conditions, market orders can fill far from the displayed price. Understanding this distinction is table stakes for reading exchange interfaces and for spotting 'free money' scams that rely on confusing order types.

title: Futures and Perpetual Contracts
content: Futures are derivative contracts to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date; perpetual contracts (perps) are futures with no expiry, using a funding rate to keep price anchored to spot. Both let traders use leverage, amplifying gains and losses. Liquidation risk means a leveraged position can be closed automatically near price swings. Perp markets often lead spot price and are a rich source of short-term signal, but they are not investment advice.

title: Leverage and Margin
content: Leverage lets a trader control a position larger than their collateral, expressed as a multiplier (e.g. 10x). Margin is the collateral posted; if the position moves against the trader past a threshold, it is liquidated. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses symmetrically, and funding/fees erode positions held over time. Most retail losses in crypto come from over-leveraged trades, not from holding spot. Never use leverage on assets you do not fully understand.

title: Liquidation
content: Liquidation is the automatic closing of a leveraged position or collateralized loan when its collateral value falls below the required threshold. On exchanges, a liquidation engine force-sells the position, often at a penalty and at unfavorable prices, and cascades of liquidations can crash prices further. For DeFi loans, a health factor below 1 triggers the same. Monitoring liquidation levels is essential risk management; surprise liquidations are a top cause of account wipeouts.

title: Funding Rate
content: The funding rate is a periodic payment between longs and shorts on perpetual futures that keeps the perp price anchored to spot. Positive funding means longs pay shorts (crowded longs); negative means shorts pay longs. Extreme funding readings signal crowded positioning and often precede reversals. Funding rates are also a sentiment gauge, but they say nothing about a token's fundamentals or scam risk — a 'funded' pump can still be a rug.

title: Wash Trading and Fake Volume
content: Wash trading is the practice of buying and selling the same asset to create the appearance of real volume. On DEXs it is easy to spot on-chain: the same wallets trading the same amounts in tight loops, or volume far exceeding holder counts. Fake volume is a standard trick in scam launches — bots generate an active-looking chart to attract victims before the exit. Check volume against holder distribution and top-trader behavior, not just the ticker.

title: Total Supply vs Circulating Supply
content: Total supply is the maximum number of tokens that exist or will ever exist; circulating supply is the portion tradeable in the market. Locked, vesting, treasury and team allocations are counted in total but not circulating. The gap matters: a token with 10% circulating and 90% locked faces massive future sell pressure as unlocks occur. Always read the unlock schedule before judging a token's valuation or scarcity narrative.

title: Vesting and Cliff
content: Vesting releases team and investor tokens gradually over time; a cliff is the initial period before any tokens unlock. Standard practice is 1-4 year linear vesting with a 6-12 month cliff. Red flags are no vesting at all, insiders unlocking within weeks of launch, or 'vesting' that can be bypassed by minting new supply. Vesting protects retail from instant insider dumps; its absence is a strong rug-pull signal.

title: Token Distribution
content: Token distribution describes how the initial supply is allocated among team, investors, community, treasury and liquidity. A healthy allocation keeps the team plus early investors under roughly 50% and gives the community a meaningful share. When insiders hold more than half of supply with no lock, they can dump on any rally. On-chain holder concentration (top 10 wallets holding 80%+) is the observable version of this risk.

title: Token Emissions and Inflation
content: Emissions are new tokens minted over time, whether as staking rewards, farming incentives or validator payouts. High emission rates dilute existing holders unless offset by burns or real revenue. Annual inflation above roughly 20% is aggressive and usually funnels to early farmers who dump. Check the emission schedule and who receives the new supply — rewards paid in tokens that insiders can mint on demand are a red flag.

title: Token Utility
content: Token utility is what a token actually does: governance voting, fee payment, staking security, gas, or claims on revenue. Governance-only tokens with no revenue share capture little value, while tokens with real cash flows (fees, buybacks) behave more like equity. Scam tokens often claim 'ecosystem utility' that does not exist on-chain. Evaluate utility by reading the contract and docs, not the marketing page.

title: Token Burn
content: A token burn permanently removes tokens from supply by sending them to an unspendable address or calling a burn function, reducing supply and potentially supporting price. Burns are only meaningful if they are real and verifiable on-chain; many projects announce 'weekly burns' that are tiny or purely cosmetic. A burn address that can still be controlled, or 'burns' that actually send tokens to an insider wallet, are scam tells.

title: Block Explorer
content: A block explorer is a web tool for reading blockchain data: balances, transactions, contract code, holders and token transfers. Etherscan, Solscan and similar explorers are the ground truth for verifying claims about a token — check the contract address, liquidity, holder distribution and transfer history directly. Scammers create fake explorers or fake explorer URLs that show invented data; always bookmark the real explorer for each chain.

title: Transaction Lifecycle
content: An on-chain transaction moves through stages: signed locally, broadcast to the network, sitting in the mempool, included in a block, and confirmed as blocks stack on top. During the mempool stage the transaction is visible to watchers, enabling front-running. Users should verify the final status on a block explorer rather than trusting a wallet popup, since a transaction can fail, be replaced, or be reorged.

title: Wallet Address Types
content: EVM addresses start with 0x and are derived from a public key; Solana addresses are base58 strings of 32-44 characters. EVM addresses can be checksummed (EIP-55 mixed case) to catch typos. Because blockchains are public ledgers, addresses are pseudonymous but traceable — clustering analysis can link wallets to each other and to exchanges. Never reuse addresses for sensitive operations, and always verify the full address, not just the first and last characters.

title: Confirmations and Reorgs
content: Each new block built on top of a block adds a confirmation. On proof-of-work chains, a reorganization (reorg) can replace recent blocks when competing chains race, so merchants wait several confirmations to prevent double-spend. Proof-of-stake chains finalize quickly once two-thirds of validators attest. Accepting zero or one confirmation for large payments is risky; scammers pressure victims to accept unconfirmed 'instant' payments.

title: Nonce and Transaction Replacement
content: The nonce is a per-address counter that numbers transactions in order; a wallet cannot submit a second transaction with the same nonce unless replacing the first (via higher gas price) or cancelling it. Stuck transactions happen when a nonce is skipped or gas is too low. On some chains, nonce gaps and pending replacements are exploitable confusion vectors in scams that show a 'sent' transaction that never confirms.

title: Token Approval and Allowance
content: Approving a token (ERC-20 allowance) lets a contract spend a specific amount of your tokens without asking again. Unlimited approvals (type(uint256).max) are convenient but dangerous: if the approved contract is compromised or malicious, it can drain your balance at any time. Scammers trick users into approving a malicious contract, then invoke the allowance later (ice phishing). Revoke unused approvals regularly using revoke.cash or similar tools.

title: Rug Pull
content: A rug pull is when developers drain a project's liquidity or dump their own token allocation, collapsing the price and leaving holders with worthless assets. Common mechanics: removing liquidity from the pool, minting and selling unlimited supply, or upgrading a contract to steal funds. Red flags include locked liquidity that is actually removable, a non-renounced owner with withdraw functions, and a deployer wallet that has launched multiple failed tokens. Severity: critical.

title: Honeypot
content: A honeypot token lets buyers purchase but prevents them from selling — only whitelisted addresses can exit. The contract typically contains transfer restrictions that revert for non-whitelisted sellers, while buy-side checks are bypassed to keep the illusion alive. Detection: simulate a buy and immediate sell; if the sell reverts, it is a honeypot. Victims discover they can never exit, and the developers sell into the buying pressure. Severity: critical.

title: Pump and Dump
content: A pump and dump inflates a token's price through coordinated buying and hype, then organizers sell at the top while victims hold the bag. On-chain tells: a small group of wallets buying in the same block at launch (bundler), hype channels shilling a token with no product, and volume collapsing once the organizers exit. The pump phase can look like genuine momentum — that is the point. Never chase tokens being shilled in group chats by anonymous accounts.

title: Phishing
content: Phishing steals credentials or wallet access through fake websites, emails, DMs or apps that impersonate legitimate services. Crypto variants include fake exchange logins, fake airdrop claim pages and fake wallet apps. A phishing page may show the real-looking interface while silently collecting your seed phrase or signing malicious transactions. Defenses: bookmark real URLs, never click links from unsolicited messages, verify domains carefully (punycode lookalikes), and use a hardware wallet.

title: Wallet Drainer
content: A wallet drainer is a malicious smart contract or dApp that tricks users into signing a transaction which transfers all approved assets to the attacker. The trick usually arrives as 'connect wallet to claim airdrop' or 'verify wallet to unstake'. The victim signs what looks like a harmless signature; the drainer then sweeps tokens, NFTs and approved balances. Approval phishing and drainers account for a large share of Web3 theft. Never sign transactions from unverified sites.

title: Fake / Impersonation Token
content: A fake token impersonates a legitimate project by copying its name, symbol and branding while using a different contract address. Buyers who do not verify the address buy the counterfeit. Detection: compare the contract address against official sources (CoinGecko, the project site), check the deployer's history for similar clones, and compare bytecode with the real token. The same impersonation technique is used for fake NFT collections and fake airdrops.

title: Fake Airdrop / Claim Scam
content: Fake airdrops promise free tokens to lure victims to a malicious claim site. The site asks the victim to 'connect wallet' (enabling a drainer) or to pay a small 'gas fee' to receive the airdrop (a direct theft). Legitimate airdrops never require payment or private keys. If something claims to be an airdrop but demands an advance fee or a wallet connection to an unknown site, treat it as a scam. Real airdrops can also be farmed, but only from official announcements.

title: Dusting Attack
content: A dusting attack sends tiny amounts of tokens to many wallets to break privacy or set up a phishing follow-up. The attacker watches when the dust is moved or consolidated, linking addresses to each other and potentially to identities. Many dust transactions carry a memo containing a malicious link. Best practice: ignore unsolicited dust, do not interact with it, and use fresh addresses for sensitive consolidation.

title: Address Poisoning
content: Address poisoning sends a zero-value or tiny transaction from an address that visually resembles one you have used, so your history shows a 'familiar' address that is actually the attacker's. When you copy the address from history instead of the source, funds go to the attacker. The prefix and suffix of real addresses are often copied exactly; only the middle differs. Always verify the full address, ideally by checksum or clipboard compare against a trusted source.

title: Ice Phishing
content: Ice phishing is a Web3 attack where a malicious site asks the victim to approve token spending or sign a transaction that gives the attacker control — often disguised as 'voting', 'claiming rewards' or 'migrating tokens'. Unlike a drainer that sweeps immediately, ice phishing may sit dormant until the victim's balance is worth taking. The transaction prompt is the attack surface: always read exactly what you are signing and verify the contract address being approved.

title: Seed Phrase Theft
content: Seed phrase theft is the direct theft of a wallet's recovery phrase through phishing, malware, fake support or social engineering. Attackers ask victims to 'verify' their phrase, type it into a fake wallet, or share it with 'support' — no legitimate service ever asks for a seed phrase. Once obtained, the phrase is used to sweep every wallet derived from it across all chains. Theft is permanent and almost never recoverable. Store phrases offline and never enter them on any website.

title: Pig Butchering / Romance Scam
content: Pig butchering is a long-con fraud where scammers build trust through dating apps or messaging, then steer the victim into a fake investment platform showing fabricated gains. Victims are encouraged to deposit more, and 'withdrawals' always fail with new fees. The platform is fake end-to-end. Warning signs: a new 'friend' pushing an investment app, profits that look too good, and pressure to deposit urgently. Real returns are never guaranteed by strangers met online.

title: Fake Support / Recovery Scam
content: Fake support scams impersonate exchanges, wallet providers or blockchain-security firms, often appearing in DMs or search ads. They 'help' with a stuck transaction or offer to 'recover stolen funds' — and ask for your seed phrase, a 'verification deposit', or remote access to your device. Legitimate support never asks for your seed phrase or a fee to unlock your own funds. 'Recovery' services that demand an upfront fee are themselves the scam.

title: Fake Exchange / Fake App
content: Fake exchanges and fake wallet apps clone a real brand to harvest deposits or keys. They may appear in app stores, as browser extensions, or via ads, and they often show real market data to look convincing. Deposits disappear and withdrawals are blocked. Defenses: download apps only from official sources and verify the developer, check the domain carefully, and test with a tiny amount before trusting any platform with real funds.

title: Giveaway Scam
content: Giveaway scams impersonate celebrities, exchanges or projects and promise to double any crypto sent to a 'promotional' address. The message usually arrives from a hacked or lookalike account, sometimes with a 'verified' badge. No legitimate entity asks you to send money to receive more. Doubling schemes are mathematically identical to theft. Report and block; never send funds to addresses advertised in comments or DMs.

title: Clipboard Hijacking
content: Clipboard hijacking malware replaces a copied wallet address with the attacker's address when you paste, so funds go to the attacker while you believe you are paying the intended recipient. It commonly arrives via fake browser extensions, cracked software or malicious downloads. Mitigations: verify the pasted address character-by-character before confirming, use address-book features, and send a small test transaction before large transfers.

title: Hardware Wallet
content: A hardware wallet keeps private keys in a secure element that never exposes them to the internet-connected device. Transactions are signed on-device after physical confirmation, so even a compromised computer cannot exfiltrate keys or sign silently. They are the strongest practical protection against phishing, malware and wallet drainers. The main risks shift to the seed-phrase backup and the physical device itself — keep the seed offline and buy hardware only from official channels.

title: Cold Storage
content: Cold storage keeps private keys fully offline — on hardware wallets, air-gapped devices or paper — so remote attackers cannot reach them. Hot wallets connected to the internet are convenient but continuously exposed. The standard practice is to keep the majority of funds in cold storage and only a small spending balance in a hot wallet. Cold storage is not immune to physical theft or seed-phrase leaks, so the backup procedure is part of the security.

title: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
content: Two-factor authentication adds a second verification step beyond a password. App-based TOTP authenticators are better than SMS 2FA, because SIM-swap attacks can redirect SMS codes to attackers. On exchanges, 2FA protects the account login, but it does not protect against withdrawal-address tampering or a compromised session. Combine 2FA with withdrawal allowlists and hardware keys where available. A password alone is never sufficient for a financial account.

title: Revoking Token Approvals
content: Revoking token approvals removes the permission a contract has to spend your tokens. Because many users leave unlimited approvals behind, a compromised or malicious contract can drain balances at any time. Periodically audit your approvals and revoke any for contracts you no longer use, using tools such as revoke.cash or the explorer's approval manager. Revoking is a cheap transaction that closes a common attack surface.

title: Smart Contract Audit
content: A smart contract audit is a security review by a third-party firm that looks for vulnerabilities, logic flaws and centralization risks. An audit is not a guarantee of safety: audits miss bugs, become outdated as code changes, and some are paid-for rubber stamps. When evaluating a token, check who audited it, read the findings (including unresolved ones), and verify the audited code matches the deployed bytecode. An unaudited contract with financial value is a red flag.

title: Verifying Contract Source
content: Contract verification publishes the source code and compiler settings on a block explorer so anyone can compare them with the deployed bytecode. Verified contracts can be inspected for hidden functions, backdoors and suspicious permissions; unverified contracts are opaque. Always read the verified source (or at minimum check for a verified label) before interacting. Automated scanners complement, but do not replace, reading the critical functions.

title: Ownership Renouncement
content: Ownership renouncement sets the contract owner to the zero address, permanently disabling owner-only functions such as minting, tax changes and withdrawals. A renounced owner is a strong decentralization signal because no single account can modify the contract. But renouncement alone is not enough: some contracts retain admin roles, or the renounced function was never the dangerous one. Verify that the actual attack surface (mint, withdraw, transfer restrictions) is genuinely locked.

title: Timelock
content: A timelock delays sensitive contract operations (upgrades, parameter changes, withdrawals) by a fixed period after they are queued, giving users time to react and exit before changes take effect. The delay must be long enough to be meaningful — hours, not seconds. A timelock controlled by a single EOA still concentrates power, just slower. Look for timelock duration, who can bypass it, and whether upgrades can be executed immediately.

title: Multisig Wallet
content: A multisig wallet requires multiple signatures to execute a transaction (e.g. 2-of-3, 3-of-5). It reduces the risk of a single compromised key and is standard for protocol treasuries and owner roles. Multisig quality depends on who holds the keys and how many: keys held by the same team on the same devices add little protection. Check signer count, signer identities and whether signatures can be added/removed by a smaller subset.

title: Social Engineering
content: Social engineering manipulates people into revealing secrets or performing actions — the most common entry point for crypto theft, ahead of technical exploits. Attackers impersonate support, admins, exchanges, or 'auditors', create urgency, and offer 'help' that requires your seed phrase or a signature. Defense is behavioral: verify identities out-of-band, never share secrets, slow down when pressured, and treat unexpected messages as suspicious by default.

title: Support and Resistance
content: Support is a price level where buying has historically been strong enough to halt declines; resistance is a level where selling halts advances. Levels strengthen with repeated tests and volume. When price breaks a level, support often becomes resistance and vice versa. Levels are probabilistic zones, not hard lines. Identifying them is foundational to TA, but beware that obvious levels are also where stop-loss hunts and liquidity grabs occur.

title: Moving Averages (SMA / EMA)
content: A moving average smooths price over a period. The simple moving average (SMA) weights all points equally; the exponential moving average (EMA) weights recent price more. The 20, 50 and 200-period averages are the most watched. Crossovers (golden cross = 50 above 200, death cross = 50 below 200) are lagging signals of trend change, not predictions. MAs also act as dynamic support/resistance and are common entry references for momentum traders.

title: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
content: The Relative Strength Index (RSI) measures the speed and magnitude of recent price moves on a 0-100 scale. Readings above 70 are conventionally 'overbought' and below 30 'oversold', but in strong trends RSI can stay extreme for long periods. Divergence — price making a new high while RSI makes a lower high — is a common reversal warning. RSI is a momentum tool, not a standalone entry signal, and it says nothing about a token's fundamental or scam risk.

title: MACD
content: The Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) indicator plots the difference between a fast and a slow EMA (typically 12 and 26) against a signal line (9-period EMA of that difference). The histogram shows the gap between MACD and signal. Crossovers and divergences are used to time trend changes and momentum shifts. MACD is lagging and prone to whipsaws in ranging markets; pair it with price structure rather than using it alone.

title: Bollinger Bands
content: Bollinger Bands draw a moving average with upper and lower bands at a set number of standard deviations (default 2). When volatility falls, the bands squeeze; squeezes often precede breakouts. Price touching a band is not itself a signal — bands describe volatility, not overbought/oversold in a fixed sense. In crypto, band squeezes on meme tokens frequently resolve with violent moves in either direction, so position sizing matters.

title: Fibonacci Retracement
content: Fibonacci retracement levels (23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, 78.6%) are drawn between a swing high and low to mark potential pullback zones in a trend. The levels are widely watched, which makes them self-fulfilling to a degree, but they are zones, not exact prices. Crypto charts also use Fibonacci extensions for targets. Like all TA, Fibonacci works best with confluence from structure, volume and other indicators.

title: Candlestick Patterns
content: Candlesticks summarize open, high, low and close per period and their bodies/wicks convey buyer-seller balance. Common signals: doji (indecision), hammer (rejection of lows), engulfing (momentum reversal) and pin bars (wicks rejecting a level). Single-candle patterns are weak alone; their value rises with location (at support/resistance) and confirmation on the next candle. Patterns on scam tokens are noise — the same chart can print bullish setups while the exit happens.

title: Head and Shoulders
content: The head and shoulders pattern has three peaks — a middle (head) higher than the two shoulders — and a neckline across the intervening lows. A close below the neckline is a classic bearish reversal signal; the inverse pattern signals a bullish reversal. Like all chart patterns, it is probabilistic and prone to false breaks, especially in manipulated crypto markets. Measure the distance from head to neckline for a rough target, but manage risk regardless.

title: Market Structure (HH/HL, LH/LL)
content: Market structure reads the sequence of swing highs and lows. Higher highs with higher lows = uptrend; lower highs with lower lows = downtrend; equal highs/lows = range. Structure breaks (a close beyond the last swing) are how trend changes are confirmed. Crypto markets frequently show structure breaks that fail immediately (liquidity grabs), so combine structure with higher-timeframe context. Structure is the least ambiguous TA concept because it is directly observable.

title: Volume Analysis
content: Volume confirms whether a price move has participation. Breakouts on rising volume are more credible; rallies on falling volume are suspect. On-chain, volume can be faked via wash trading, so cross-check DEX volume against holder counts and top-trader behavior. Volume profile shows traded volume at each price level, marking high-volume nodes that act as support/resistance. In scam tokens, volume is often manufactured to lure momentum buyers.

title: Divergence
content: Divergence occurs when price and an oscillator (RSI, MACD, momentum) move in opposite directions. Bearish divergence: price makes a higher high while the oscillator makes a lower high — momentum is fading. Bullish divergence is the mirror. Divergence warns of potential reversals but can persist in strong trends; it is a timing filter, not a signal to trade against the trend blindly. On thinly traded tokens, divergence readings are unreliable due to price manipulation.

title: Order Blocks
content: Order blocks are zones where large institutional orders previously rested, visible as the last opposing candle(s) before a strong directional move. Buyers' order blocks sit before sharp up-moves; sellers' order blocks before sharp down-moves. Price often returns to these zones ('liquidity sweeps') before continuing. Order blocks overlap with supply/demand zones and are a core concept in modern price-action trading. In thinly traded meme tokens, what looks like an order block is often a single whale's wall that can vanish instantly, so treat them as probability zones, not guarantees.

title: Trendlines
content: A trendline connects successive swing lows (uptrend) or swing highs (downtrend) and acts as dynamic support or resistance. A valid trendline needs at least two confirmed touches and gains strength with each additional touch. A break of a trendline signals possible trend change but frequently produces false breaks, especially in low-liquidity crypto. Trendlines are subjective: different analysts draw them differently. Combine with volume and higher-timeframe structure before treating a break as real.

title: Liquidity Zones and Stop Hunts
content: Liquidity accumulates where many traders place stop losses and where institutions can fill large orders: above obvious highs and below obvious lows. Algorithms often push price into these zones to trigger stops before reversing — a 'stop hunt' or 'liquidity sweep'. Understanding liquidity zones explains why price routinely spikes beyond support and resistance before moving in the intended direction. In low-volume tokens, a single wallet can engineer fake liquidity sweeps to manipulate traders, so liquidity analysis on-chain is safer than on the chart alone.

title: Accumulation and Distribution
content: Accumulation is a sideways range in which informed buyers quietly build positions; distribution is the mirror phase in which holders sell into strength. Classic Wyckoff theory describes accumulation (springs, test of supply) and distribution (upthrusts) as the phases before markup and markdown. On-chain signals help confirm the phase: flat price with rising exchange outflows suggests accumulation, while flat price with heavy exchange inflows suggests distribution. For scam tokens, 'accumulation' patterns are often engineered by wash trading, so verify volume authenticity.

title: Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)
content: VWAP is the average price a token traded at, weighted by volume, typically over a session or since listing. Institutions use it to benchmark execution: buying below VWAP and selling above it is considered good execution. As a technical level, VWAP acts as intraday support/resistance and mean-reversion magnet. On-chain VWAP built from DEX pool data is more trustworthy than exchange charts because it cannot be gamed by a single venue's fake volume. Deviation from VWAP can flag manipulated prints in wash-traded tokens.

title: Average True Range (ATR)
content: ATR measures the average true range of price movement over a lookback window and quantifies volatility, not direction. High ATR means wide candles and large swings; low ATR means quiet, compressed price. ATR is used to size stops (e.g. 1.5-2x ATR below entry) and to scale position size to volatility. Meme tokens routinely print extreme ATR, so stops sized from a calm period get run over instantly. ATR does not signal trend or reversal — it is a volatility gauge, best combined with structure and volume.

title: Chart Patterns
content: Chart patterns are recognizable price formations: flags and pennants (continuation), triangles (compression before breakout), double tops and bottoms (reversal), head-and-shoulders (reversal), and wedges. Patterns are probabilistic, not deterministic — a breakout fails roughly half the time without volume confirmation. Crypto is pattern-rich partly because of retail flow and bots, but also because wash traders can draw fake patterns on low-liquidity tokens. Validate any pattern with volume, higher-timeframe context, and on-chain holder behavior before acting.

title: Price Action
content: Price action trading reads raw candlestick formations and swing structure without relying on lagging indicators. Core signals are market structure (higher highs/lows), rejection wicks, engulfing candles, and closes relative to key levels. Price action is the most direct read of supply and demand, but it is also the easiest to fake in manipulated markets: one wallet can paint wicks and headers on a thin pool. The most robust approach combines price action with on-chain checks — holder concentration, LP status, and volume authenticity.

title: Multi-Timeframe Analysis
content: Multi-timeframe analysis reads the same market across timeframes: the daily defines the trend, the 4h/1h defines the setup, and the lower timeframe defines entry timing. Trading with the higher-timeframe trend dramatically improves win rate because entries align with the dominant flow. The common failure is trading a 1m entry against a daily downtrend. For low-cap tokens, higher timeframes are often too empty to read, so combine with on-chain signals: holder counts, liquidity depth, and top-trader behavior substitute for missing chart context.

title: Momentum
content: Momentum measures the rate of price change over time, typically with indicators like rate of change (ROC), MACD, or RSI. Strong momentum in the direction of the trend increases the odds of continuation; fading momentum warns of exhaustion. Momentum is a leading feel for trend health but a lagging trigger for entries. In crypto, momentum can be manufactured: wash trading and spoofed walls create fake acceleration. Confirm momentum with real volume and holder growth, especially for tokens whose only story is 'going up'.

title: Volume Profile
content: Volume profile shows how much volume traded at each price level over a period, marking high-volume nodes (HVN) that act as magnets and support/resistance, and low-volume nodes (LVN) that price passes through quickly. Unlike time-based indicators, it is price-centric: it reveals where the market actually exchanged hands. The point of control (POC) is the highest-volume price. On DEXs, volume profile computed from pool swaps is meaningful, but beware wash-traded volume inflating nodes — cross-check against holder count and top-trader flow.

title: Consolidation and Breakouts
content: Consolidation is a tightening range where buyers and sellers pause; a breakout is the subsequent move beyond the range. Breakouts on rising volume are more credible, while breakouts on falling volume often fail and 'retest' the range. The trap in crypto is the fake breakout: bots or a whale push price beyond resistance, trigger stops, then reverse. Wait for a close beyond the level and volume confirmation, and check the LP for depth before a breakout — a thin pool breaks out in both directions with equal ease.

title: Maximal Extractable Value (MEV)
content: MEV is the profit validators, searchers, and bots extract by ordering, inserting, or censoring transactions inside a block. Common MEV strategies are front-running (copying a pending trade ahead of it), back-running, sandwich attacks, and liquidations. MEV taxes regular users via worse prices and failed transactions. It is concentrated on public-mempool EVM chains; Solana's ordering differs but MEV still exists via priority fees. Projects mitigate MEV with private mempools, intents, and fair-ordering protocols. MEV risk is highest around large swaps and new token launches.

title: Sandwich Attack
content: A sandwich attack is an MEV strategy where a bot places a buy order right before a victim's large swap and a sell right after, profiting from the price impact the victim's trade causes. The victim buys high and sells low relative to the market. High-slippage swaps on thin pools are prime targets. Protection includes setting tight slippage, using private RPCs, and avoiding swaps on tokens with shallow liquidity. On low-liquidity meme tokens, sandwiching is rampant and is one reason executed prices differ so much from quoted prices.

title: Arbitrage
content: Arbitrage is buying an asset where it is cheaper and selling where it is more expensive, capturing the price difference. In DeFi, bots arbitrage between DEX pools, CEXs, and bridge quotes, which is what keeps prices roughly consistent across venues. Retail arbitrage between venues is usually unprofitable after fees, gas, and slippage. Cross-chain and bridge arbitrage carries additional risk: bridge lags and fake wrapped assets can turn a 'risk-free' arb into a loss. When a token trades at wildly different prices across venues, check whether liquidity is real or the spread is a scam artifact.

title: Total Value Locked (TVL)
content: TVL is the total value of assets deposited into a protocol, a headline metric for DeFi adoption. It is frequently misleading: TVL can be inflated with the protocol's own token, double-counted across layers, or boosted by short-term farming incentives that leave the day the rewards end. For scam assessment, a token's own price collapse does not need a TVL collapse — TVL is a usage signal, not a safety signal. Always check what proportion of TVL is the protocol's own token versus real external assets.

title: Concentrated Liquidity
content: Concentrated liquidity (Uniswap v3-style) lets LPs provide liquidity inside a custom price range instead of 0 to infinity, earning higher fees per dollar when the price stays in range. The tradeoff is that when price exits the range, the position converts to a single asset and stops earning. Managing concentrated positions is active work: ranges need rebalancing as price moves. For LPs it concentrates impermanent-loss risk exactly where price is most volatile. Scrutinize projects that advertise 'high APY' from concentrated liquidity — the yield usually comes from increased risk, not magic.

title: Rebase Tokens
content: A rebase token adjusts its supply algorithmically at intervals so each holder's balance scales while the wallet balance stays fixed. Positive rebases expand supply (diluting price); negative rebases contract supply. The total value of a holder's position is unchanged by the rebase itself — rebasing is cosmetic unless demand follows. The infamous OHM forks used rebase to manufacture high 'APY' that was paid in newly minted supply. If a token claims massive rebase APY, ask where the real yield comes from; usually it is new supply entering the market.

title: Algorithmic Stablecoins
content: An algorithmic stablecoin keeps its peg without full fiat or crypto collateral backing, relying instead on arbitrage and supply expansion/contraction. The canonical failure is a death spiral: when confidence drops, holders sell, supply expands further, price falls more, and the 'stablecoin' collapses toward zero (LUNA/UST, 2022). Partial-collateral models are safer than pure algorithmic ones but still fragile in stress. Any stablecoin whose peg is defended only by an arbitrage mechanism and its own token is high risk. Verify reserves, collateralization, and whether the issuer can actually honor redemptions.

title: DEX Aggregators
content: A DEX aggregator splits one swap across many pools and routes to the best combined price, improving fills and reducing slippage. Aggregators also expose extra risk: routing through obscure or unaudited pools, and executing with insufficient slippage checks. A token may appear 'listed' on an aggregator when it is only available in a scam pool the aggregator vacuously routes through. Always verify the actual pool and pair an aggregator routed, not just the displayed price. Aggregator quotes are a starting point; the executed route defines the real risk.

title: veTokenomics (Vote-Escrowed Tokens)
content: veTokenomics (Curve-style vote-escrowed tokens) lock protocol tokens for up to four years in exchange for governance voting power and boosted rewards. Locking reduces circulating supply and aligns holders with long-term protocol health, but it also creates large illiquid positions and governance capture risks: a few ve holders can steer emissions to their own pools. For a token analysis, ve models reward lockers at the expense of new entrants, so 'low inflation' headlines can mask heavy distribution to early lockers. Assess who actually controls ve voting before trusting the model.

title: Lending Protocol Risks
content: DeFi lending protocols let users supply assets to earn yield and borrow against collateral. Risks include oracle failures (a manipulated price liquidating positions), cascading liquidations in volatile markets, and protocol insolvency when bad debt exceeds reserves. Borrowers face liquidation penalties and rapid position closures during drawdowns. Lenders face shortfall risk when undercollateralized loans cannot be recovered. Before lending to a protocol, check the collateral factors, oracle sources, and historical stress behavior. High supply APY is often a signal that borrowers are paying a lot to take on risk.

title: DeFi Liquidations
content: Liquidation closes a borrower's position when collateral drops below the health threshold, selling collateral (often at a discount) to repay the loan. Liquidation cascades happen when many leveraged positions share the same price feed: one liquidation drives price down, triggering more. MEV bots race to liquidate first and capture the discount, making liquidations fast and ruthless. For leveraged traders, liquidation price is the number that matters — most crypto losses on leverage come from underestimating how quickly cascades move. Check a token's open-interest and leverage ratio before assuming a 'dip' is buyable.

title: DeFi Borrowing and Collateral
content: DeFi borrowing lets users lock collateral (usually over-collateralized) to borrow stablecoins or other assets without a credit check. Health factor = collateral value / borrow value; dropping below 1 triggers liquidation. Over-collateralization means borrowing is capital-inefficient but protocol-safe, while under-collateralized or zero-collateral loans depend on the protocol's own token or social trust — the riskier design. When analyzing a token, large amounts of its supply locked as collateral can artificially tighten float; a collateral unwind can then flood supply. Track collateral composition as a supply risk signal.

title: Perpetual Futures (Perps)
content: Perpetual futures are derivative contracts with no expiry that track an underlying asset via a funding rate: longs pay shorts (or vice versa) periodically to keep the price near spot. Perps enable high leverage and are where most crypto liquidations happen. Funding rate is a sentiment gauge — persistently high positive funding means crowded longs. Perp price can diverge from spot, especially in illiquid assets. Scam tokens use 'listed on a perp venue' as a legitimacy signal; verify actual volume and open interest, since some venues list anything for a fee.

title: Reentrancy
content: Reentrancy is a smart-contract vulnerability where a function calls an external contract before updating its own state, allowing the callee to re-enter the same function while the state is stale and drain funds repeatedly. The 2016 DAO hack and numerous bridges were reentrancy exploits. Mitigations: checks-effects-interactions ordering, reentrancy guards, and pull-over-push payment patterns. When auditing a contract, look for external calls before state updates and for custom fallback functions. Reentrancy is the most famous class of smart-contract bug precisely because it is simple to write and devastating in impact.

title: Flash Loan Attacks
content: A flash loan is an uncollateralized loan borrowed and repaid within the same transaction. Attackers use flash loans to obtain massive capital for an exploit without owning it: manipulate an oracle, drain a pool, or arbitrage a pricing bug, then repay the loan in the same block. The flash loan itself is not the vulnerability — it is the amplifier that turns a small pricing defect into a full protocol drain. When a protocol is exploited for millions with tiny TVL, a flash loan is usually involved. Audits must test oracle pricing and invariant checks against flash-loan-sized capital.

title: Oracle Manipulation
content: Oracle manipulation is feeding a protocol false price data so it makes decisions at the attacker's advantage. In its simplest form, an attacker with a large bag manipulates a thin DEX pool's spot price, then borrows or liquidates against the fake price before it normalizes. TWAP oracles and multiple independent sources resist single-block manipulation; spot-price oracles on thin pools do not. Every DeFi exploit that 'borrowed against a fake price' was oracle manipulation. When assessing a token, check which oracle feeds its lending/derivative integrations and how deep the referenced pools are.

title: Front-Running (Transaction Ordering)
content: Front-running is when an attacker sees a pending transaction in the mempool and places their own transaction first to profit from the victim's move — buying before a large buy, selling before a large sell. On public EVM chains every pending swap is visible to bots. Protections include private RPCs, commit-reveal schemes, and anti-front-running AMM designs. For token analysis, large pending buys are routinely front-run by MEV bots, so a 'whale is buying' signal on-chain is often already stale. Slippage tolerance and deadlines limit the damage.

title: Access Control
content: Access control vulnerabilities let unauthorized users call privileged functions. In tokens, the classic version is an owner or 'minter' role that can mint unlimited supply, pause trading, or modify fees and taxes. Missing role checks let anyone call admin functions. A key rug-pull mechanism is a role that was renounced publicly but still reachable through an upgradeable proxy or a second hidden admin. Audit checklist: enumerate every privileged function, who can call it, and whether the admin key is a wallet, a timelock, or a dead address. Centralized control is not automatically a scam, but it is the primary rug vector.

title: Unchecked External Calls
content: Unchecked external calls ignore the return value or failure of a call to another contract. In Solidity, low-level calls return a boolean success flag that must be checked; ignoring it can leave the protocol state inconsistent, let an attacker complete a flow that should have failed, or allow funds to be sent to a contract that silently rejects them. Related to this is using transfer()/send() with fixed gas, which can brick payments as gas costs rise. Audit pattern: every external interaction must handle failure explicitly, and interactions should follow checks-effects-interactions.

title: Integer Overflow and Underflow
content: Integer overflow/underflow occurs when arithmetic wraps past the type's limits — pre-0.8 Solidity silently wrapped, letting a balance become astronomically large or a subtraction underflow to near-max supply. Solidity 0.8+ reverts by default, but unchecked blocks, casts, and non-EVM chains can still wrap. Attack patterns: minting via overflow, bypassing balance checks, or corrupting accounting. Audit checklist: look for arithmetic on balances, allowances, and token amounts, and for any unchecked or cast operations. Overflow bugs are less common now but still appear in bridges and custom VMs.

title: Upgradeable Contract Risks
content: Upgradeable contracts use a proxy that delegates calls to an implementation contract, letting the owner swap the logic after deployment. This is a double-edged sword: it enables bug fixes, and it enables rug pulls — an owner can upgrade to a contract that steals balances or blocks sells. The 2021 Poly Network and many bridge hacks were upgrade-based. When a token is upgradeable, the admin key IS the protocol's security: if it is a single wallet, the token can be rugpulled at any moment regardless of what the current code says. Verify the proxy owner and whether any timelock protects upgrades.

title: Proxy Patterns (EIP-1967, Beacon)
content: Proxy patterns separate storage (proxy) from logic (implementation) so contracts can be upgraded without moving state. Common variants are transparent proxies, UUPS, and beacon proxies, standardized around EIP-1967 storage slots. Proxy risks: storage collisions between proxy and implementation, uninitialized implementation contracts that an attacker can claim, and functions that can be called on the proxy directly bypassing the implementation. Auditors verify the implementation is initialized, the proxy admin is controlled, and storage layout is preserved across upgrades. For token safety, the proxy admin is the attack surface — check who owns it.

title: Signature Malleability
content: Signature malleability lets an attacker alter a valid ECDSA signature (changing s to s' or using the alternate curve point) and still produce a signature that verifies for the same message. If a protocol uses the raw signature bytes as an identifier or dedup key, a malleated copy can bypass replay protection or allow double-claiming. Mitigations: use ecrecover and check the s value, use a canonical signature encoding (EIP-2), or use EIP-712 typed data with nonces. This bug class appears in airdrop claims, multi-sig transactions, and bridges that hash raw signatures.

title: Denial of Service (DoS) in Contracts
content: Smart-contract DoS blocks the protocol from functioning: an attacker griefs a contract into an unusable state. Examples: making an external call that always fails so the contract cannot proceed (e.g. transferring to a contract that rejects ETH), front-running a required initialization, or bloating a data structure to make operations exceed gas. Token-specific DoS: a blacklist that bricks a necessary function, or a fee-on-transfer token that breaks pool integrations. DoS is not a direct fund theft but can lock user funds indefinitely. Audit checklist: every loop, every required external call, every initialization is a DoS candidate.

title: Token Approval Exploits
content: Token approval exploits abuse ERC-20/ERC-721 approve() mechanics: users grant a contract or spender allowance, and a compromised or malicious spender drains that allowance. Attack vectors: unlimited approvals to a vulnerable DEX/router, phishing sites that request approve for a malicious contract, and old approvals to exploited protocols. The standard mitigation is revoking unused approvals and using per-transaction allowances. On-chain forensics of drained wallets almost always show an approval transaction before the theft. Never approve a contract you cannot verify; check allowance on explorers and revoke via revoke.cash-style tools.

title: Liquidity Removal and LP Theft
content: Liquidity removal is the core rug-pull mechanic: the deployer withdraws the LP tokens from the pool, leaving holders with tokens nobody can sell. Variants: unlocking 'locked' liquidity early, using an unverified lock contract, or removing liquidity through a hidden function. Even locked LP is not safe if the deployer can mint new supply and dump it into the pool. When checking a token: verify the LP is actually locked (not just claimed), verify the lock contract, check whether the deployer can call removeLiquidity, and confirm supply cannot be minted. LP status is the single most important on-chain rug signal.

title: Mint Function Abuse
content: Mint abuse is the unguarded or hidden ability to create new token supply. A contract with a public or owner-only mint function lets the deployer inflate supply at will, dumping new tokens into the pool or onto holders. Warning signs: a 'max supply' that is not enforced, a mint function hidden behind an unverified implementation, or an upgrade path that adds minting later. Even with renounced ownership, a mint key inside an upgradeable contract can reappear. Always verify: can anyone mint, who can call it, and is the max supply actually capped in code?

title: Rug Pull Taxonomy
content: Rug pulls fall into recognizable classes: (1) liquidity removal — pulling LP so nothing can be sold; (2) supply manipulation — minting/dumping hidden supply; (3) contract upgrade — swapping logic to steal or block; (4) honeypot — disabling sells for most holders; (5) fake project — no real product, just marketing and a drainer; (6) insider dump — team and insiders dumping locked or pre-mined allocations. Most rugs combine two or more. The taxonomy drives detection: each class has a concrete on-chain fingerprint — LP lock status, mint authority, proxy admin, transfer restrictions, deployer history, and allocation concentration.

title: Token Buybacks
content: A buyback is when a project uses revenue or treasury funds to buy its own token, usually to burn it or reward holders. Buybacks reduce circulating supply and signal that the project has real cash flow. Red flags: buybacks funded by newly minted tokens (circular), announced but never executed, or used to prop the price before an insider dump. Unlike vesting, buybacks are discretionary — check whether the mechanism is enforceable in code or just a promise. A 'deflationary buyback' token that mints more than it buys back is marketing, not economics.

title: Inflation and Dilution
content: Inflation is new token supply entering circulation over time — through emissions, rewards, or minting — and it dilutes existing holders unless offset by demand or burns. A token's inflation schedule matters more than its headline total supply: 1% annual inflation is healthy; 100% monthly is a wealth transfer to whoever receives the emissions. Compare inflation against protocol revenue: a token that inflates faster than it earns is a claim on future buyers, not a store of value. Check both the emission rate and who the new supply flows to (team, stakers, or the market).

title: Token Velocity
content: Token velocity is how fast tokens change hands. High velocity is bad for a store-of-value token: a token that is spent immediately circulates back to sellers, suppressing price, while a token that is held or locked supports price. Velocity explains why 'useful' tokens can underperform 'useless but locked' ones. Projects reduce velocity with staking, vesting, and utility that requires holding. In scam analysis, fabricated volume inflates apparent velocity — a token 'traded' heavily by the same wallets looks active but has no real demand. Measure velocity against real holder behavior, not just swap counts.

title: Token Lockups
content: A lockup is a contractual or on-chain restriction preventing token sales for a set period. Lockups protect markets from immediate insider dumps, but they are only as strong as the enforcement: 'locked' tokens in a contract the deployer can unlock, or locks that expire with no cliff after, still hit the market eventually. The real question is what happens when the lock expires — a giant unlock is a supply overhang that suppresses price. Red flags are lockups that are unverifiable on-chain, and 'team tokens locked' claims that cannot be confirmed on the explorer.

title: Treasury Management
content: A treasury is the pool of assets a protocol controls — its own token, stablecoins, and revenue. A healthy treasury is diversified (not mostly its own token), has clear spending rules, and is audited; a treasury stuffed with the project's own token is circular — it looks rich but collapses with the token price. Treasury actions (buys, sells, grants) directly move the token. For risk assessment, check who controls the treasury, whether multi-sig and timelock protect it, and how much of it is self-referential. A treasury that exists to 'back' a stablecoin is only as good as its real assets.

title: Airdrop Farming
content: Airdrop farming is interacting with a protocol specifically to qualify for a future token airdrop. Real airdrops reward genuine usage; farmed airdrops reward sybil clusters — and the eventual dump of farmed allocations creates sell pressure. For analysts, airdrop farming distorts on-chain metrics: TVL and unique users spike before the snapshot then collapse after. Scam variants: fake airdrop sites that drain wallets, and 'airdrop' tokens that require an approval to claim. When evaluating a token, separate organic usage from farmed usage, and never connect a wallet to airdrop claim sites you cannot verify.

title: Token Sale Models (ICO, IDO, IEO)
content: Token sales raise capital in exchange for tokens: ICOs (initial coin offerings, mostly unregulated), IDOs (launches on DEX launchpads), and IEOs (launches via exchanges). Each has different investor protections — IEOs have the most gatekeeping, ICOs the least. Sale model risks: tokens sold with a 'private sale' discount that dumps on public buyers, sale contracts with hidden fees, and launches where insiders buy the public allocation. The sale structure defines early distribution — a token that is 60% insider and 40% public from day one behaves very differently from a fair launch. Read the allocation before reading the hype.

title: Fair Launch
content: A fair launch distributes tokens without privileged pre-sales or insider allocations — typically via liquidity bootstrapping, public minting, or mining from day one. Fair launches are marketed as egalitarian, but they can still be gamed: bots and whales snipe the launch, the deployer keeps a hidden allocation, or the 'fair' mint has a backdoor. The fair-launch label is a claim, not a property; verify with on-chain data (deployer balance, initial LP, mint function). For meme tokens, fair launch plus burned LP plus renounced ownership is the closest thing to a 'safe' launch pattern — and it is still risky.

title: Staking Rewards
content: Staking rewards pay token holders for locking or delegating tokens. Reward sources matter: real yield comes from protocol revenue; fake yield comes from minting new supply or from other stakers' principal. A staking APY higher than the protocol's actual revenue is a Ponzi treadmill — early stakers get paid from later deposits. Staking also reduces sellable supply, which can temporarily support price, but the moment rewards stop or unlock, supply returns. Check: what funds the rewards, the staking lock period, and whether the staking contract is upgradeable or can be drained.

title: Token Allocation
content: Token allocation is how the initial supply is split: team, investors, treasury, ecosystem, community, and public. The allocation tells you who holds the power to dump. Concentrated allocation to team and insiders (50%+) is the classic rug setup; a large 'ecosystem' or 'marketing' bucket is often a disguised insider wallet. The unlock schedule matters as much as the split — 60% to team is dangerous even with vesting if the vesting is bypassable. On-chain verification beats whitepaper claims: trace the deployer and top holder wallets and compare against the stated allocation.

title: Community and Ecosystem Funds
content: A community or ecosystem fund is a reserved allocation meant to grow the project — grants, incentives, partnerships. These funds are frequently mislabeled insider allocations or dumping grounds: the 'ecosystem' wallet sells gradually while the team denies selling. Check the fund wallet's actual behavior on-chain: outflow frequency, destination wallets, and whether the fund is controlled by a multi-sig or a single key. An ecosystem fund that starts selling near the token's peak is a top signal. Treat any large reserved bucket as potential sell pressure until the on-chain record says otherwise.

title: Deflationary Token Mechanics
content: Deflationary mechanics reduce supply over time: burns (removing tokens), fees that buy-and-burn, and rebase contractions. Deflation only helps holders if demand is stable — burning 1% while emitting 5% is net inflationary. Common scams wrap deflation in misleading language: 'auto-burn' that burns only from sellers (a disguised tax), burns of tokens the project minted for free, or 'deflationary' tokens whose supply is still controlled by a mint key. Compute the NET supply trajectory (mints minus burns) on-chain instead of trusting the marketing. A deflationary narrative with a live mint function is a contradiction.

title: Order Book
content: An order book is the real-time list of resting buy (bid) and sell (ask) orders at each price level on a central-limit-order-book venue (CEX, some perp DEXs). It reveals supply and demand at each price. Spoofing — placing large fake orders then canceling them — is a common manipulation on order books, especially in crypto where regulation is light. Book depth can vanish between snapshots, so thin books are unreliable. Order-book venues contrast with AMMs, where price comes from pool reserves. Always check the book's real depth behind the displayed bid/ask, and beware tokens with a 'CEX listing' but an empty book.

title: Maker vs Taker
content: In exchange fees, a maker adds liquidity by placing a resting order that does not execute immediately; a taker removes liquidity by crossing the spread and executing against resting orders. Makers usually pay lower (or negative) fees because they provide liquidity; takers pay the standard fee. High-frequency market makers earn rebates by quoting both sides. The maker-taker split matters for token analysis because it drives wash trading: wash traders can churn volume at maker rates to fabricate activity. When volume numbers look too big for the visible order flow, ask how much of it was maker-side rebate churn.

title: Bid-Ask Spread
content: The bid-ask spread is the gap between the best buy price and the best sell price. It is the market maker's compensation and the trader's immediate cost: buy at ask, sell at bid, and you lose the spread. Wide spreads signal illiquidity and risk; tight spreads signal healthy two-sided markets. In crypto, spreads widen violently in volatility and for low-cap tokens. On AMMs the analog is price impact — the difference between quote and fill grows with trade size. A token with a wide spread is expensive to trade and easy to manipulate; check the spread before sizing any position.

title: Market Depth
content: Market depth is the cumulative size of resting orders at each price level beyond the best bid/ask. A market is 'deep' if large orders move price little; 'shallow' if a small order causes a big move. Depth is the real liquidity measure behind the headline volume figure. In crypto, depth is frequently illusory: spoofed walls disappear on approach, and on AMMs depth equals pool reserves, which can be withdrawn. Always size trades against actual depth, not the 24h volume number. A token with $10M reported volume but $5k of real depth is a trap.

title: Iceberg and Hidden Orders
content: An iceberg order displays only a small slice of a much larger order, hiding the full size to avoid moving the market. Hidden and iceberg orders let large players accumulate or distribute without revealing their hand. On-chain, the analog is a whale splitting swaps across many addresses and venues. For token analysis, visible book depth understates large-player interest; conversely, an 'empty' book can hide a whale about to distribute. Icebergs also enable wash behavior — same wallet slicing orders to look like organic flow. Watch cumulative flow, not single orders.

title: Open Interest (OI)
content: Open interest is the total number of outstanding derivative contracts (futures/perps) that have not been settled. Rising OI with rising price confirms the trend (new money in); rising OI with falling price warns of crowded shorts or longs about to be squeezed; falling OI means positions are closing and the move is unwinding. OI spikes just before liquidation cascades. For tokens with perp listings, OI-to-market-cap ratio reveals how leveraged the market is — extreme OI relative to float is a crash risk. OI is a market-structure metric, not a fundamental one.

title: Market Impact
content: Market impact is how much a trade moves the price purely because of its size — the difference between the pre-trade quote and the average executed price. Impact grows with trade size and shrinks with liquidity. Institutional traders break large orders into small pieces to reduce impact; retail traders ignore it and get filled at terrible prices on thin tokens. On AMMs, impact is deterministic (the constant-product curve); on order books, it depends on resting depth. Impact is a direct liquidity tax: a token you cannot buy or sell without moving the price 5% is not liquid enough to trade safely.

title: Stop Orders
content: A stop order becomes a market order when price reaches a trigger level — used to cap losses or enter on breakout. Stops cluster at obvious levels (round numbers, swing highs/lows), and that clustering is what stop hunts exploit: price spikes through the level to trigger stops, then reverses. In crypto with thin books and funding-driven leverage, stop cascades can gap price far past the trigger. On AMMs there are no stops — 'stop loss' means manually swapping or setting limit orders, which adds latency in a crash. Use stops sized to real volatility, not round numbers.

title: Dark Pools and OTC Markets
content: Dark pools and OTC desks execute large trades off the public order book, avoiding market impact and public disclosure. In crypto, OTC desks and RFQ venues (request-for-quote) serve whales and institutions moving size. Dark liquidity explains puzzling behavior: a token can look quiet on-chain while large positions quietly change hands off-exchange, or a whale can exit without moving the chart — until the OTC buyer dumps on the market. For forensics, OTC trades are invisible to standard flow analysis; match wallet movements and exchange deposits instead of relying on visible volume.

title: Liquidity Provision and Market Making
content: Liquidity provision supplies tradable inventory on both sides of a market. On AMMs it means depositing token pairs into pools; on order books it means quoting bids and asks. Professional market makers earn the spread and fees but carry inventory risk — a token that moves against them can destroy their PnL. For tokens, 'liquidity provided by a market maker' is a double-edged signal: it improves tradability, but the MM can withdraw or dump inventory, and some 'market makers' are the deployer's own wallets adding fake depth. Verify who actually provides liquidity and what their historical behavior is.

title: Order Flow
content: Order flow is the real-time stream of orders and trades — who is buying, who is selling, at what size. Flow analysis separates informed activity (large, deliberate, dark) from retail noise. In crypto, on-chain order flow is unusually transparent: every swap is public, so flow can be attributed to wallets, not just venues. The signature skill is classifying flow: sniper buys at launch, accumulation patterns, and distribution dumps all have distinguishable on-chain footprints. Wash trading corrupts raw flow — always filter for self-trades and same-cluster wallets before trusting a flow read.

title: Automated Market Maker (AMM)
content: An automated market maker (AMM) is a smart-contract exchange that prices assets algorithmically from pooled reserves instead of matching buyer and seller orders. The constant-product formula (x*y=k) means price moves with the ratio of the two assets in the pool. Anyone can be a liquidity provider by depositing both assets. AMMs made permissionless trading possible but introduced new risks: impermanent loss, price impact, and pool manipulation. Uniswap, Raydium, and PancakeSwap are AMMs. The pool's reserve size determines how much a trade moves the price.

title: Oracle
content: An oracle brings off-chain data — prices, weather, sports results, exchange rates — on-chain so smart contracts can react to the real world. Price oracles are the most critical: DeFi lending, derivatives, and liquidations all depend on accurate price data. Decentralized oracles (Chainlink-style) aggregate from many sources; spot oracles read a single pool's price and are easy to manipulate. The security of a protocol often reduces to the security of its oracle. When a token integrates price feeds, ask who provides them and whether manipulation of the underlying pools could move the feed.

title: Fork Detection
content: Fork detection identifies whether a new token is a copy of an existing project — same contract pattern, same source code, or a slightly renamed clone. Forking is legal and common (most meme coins fork standard templates), but forked code inherits all the parent's vulnerabilities, and 'new' projects that fork without disclosing it are usually low-effort launches. Detection methods: comparing verified source code, matching bytecode similarity, and checking deployer history for the same template. A fork of a safe standard token is not automatically safe; a fork of an exploited contract is a trap.

title: Contract Decompilation
content: Decompilation recovers readable pseudocode from compiled bytecode when source code is not verified — the standard technique for analyzing unverified tokens. Tools like Panopticon, Pytheas, and online decompilers reconstruct functions, storage layouts, and logic. Decompiled code is harder to read than source and can hide intent (obfuscated functions, string-obfuscated addresses), but key patterns — mint calls, transfer restrictions, owner checks — are still identifiable. For scam analysis, decompilation answers the critical question: can the deployer mint, block sells, or withdraw? When a token refuses to verify source, decompile it before trusting it.
